title: Law firm with ties to Trump administration declines offer to represent migrant children
description: A small Texas law firm with ties to the Trump administration declined a $150 million federal contract it was offered to represent migrant children traveling alone to the U.S., authorities said Wednesd...
fullText:
McALLEN, Texas (AP) — A small Texas law firm with ties to the Trump administration declined a $150 million federal contract it was offered to represent migrant children traveling alone to the U.S., authorities said Wednesday, raising long-term questions about who would represent them.

The administration last week announced plans to award the contract to the Burke Law Group, a Houston-based firm with little experience in immigration. The contract offer came as the administration ramps up its mass deportation campaign and after it let a key contract with nearly 100 providers working with immigrant children around the country expire at the end of July with no replacement.

Unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody are being temporarily represented by another group, but it is unclear how things will shake out after its contract expires in December. A Wednesday statement from the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement, which oversees the contracts, offered no insight into why Burke declined the offer.

"Burke Law Group has declined to apply and has not been awarded any grant," the agency, which is part of the Department of Health and Human Services, said in an emailed statement in response to a query about the contract.

Burke Law Group published a short statement on social media Tuesday night saying it had considered applying for a "small portion" of the contract. It did not explain why it decided against it.

Burke Law Group's founder, Marcella Burke, served in President Donald Trump's first administration as a lawyer with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior.

Others on its roster include Justin Shubow, a supporter of Trump's efforts to require federal buildings to adhere to classical and traditional architectural styles, and a former Trump appointee to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. Prominent conservative legal scholar Ilya Shapiro is listed as senior counsel.

Migrant children who are detained after entering the U.S. without their parents are usually entrusted to federal government care. Congress created various legal protections for them, including the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, which requires the government to provide legal representation for children put into deportation proceedings.

About 1,800 children were living in shelters and roughly 22,000 facing deportation were living with outside sponsors such as family members, according to the legal service providers whose contract expired.

The Burke Law Group, with fewer than 30 lawyers and only two with relevant immigration experience listed on its website, was one of two groups tapped by the government to fill in the gap.

A temporary contract for $20 million was awarded through the end of the year to the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, a legal aid group whose previous work with the government involved helping resettle Afrikaners.

Attorneys with USCRI started showing up in immigration court last week, unannounced, claiming to represent children they had not yet met and sparking confusion among judges and lawyers from the expired contract still providing representation.

Some legal aid providers whose contracts expired sued the administration after they went without payment since last year. On Aug. 6, a California federal judge ordered the federal government to pay the providers.

"These half-baked plans are not sufficient to comply with this court's order," Caelin Moriarity Miltko, an attorney representing the providers, told the judge last week, referring to the interim contracts the government is trying to set up.

"Plaintiffs have ethical obligations to the children they represent today, to continue providing that representation to the best of their abilities, and that representation cannot transfer instantaneously to a new group simply because defendants have changed the contract," Miltko said.

Bilal Askaryar, director of communications at Acacia Center for Justice, the organization that handled the expired contract with the government, confirmed on Wednesday that the groups started to receive payments covering six out of nine months owed, with the rest in progress.

title: Despite minimal promotion by ESPN, Jimmy Pitaro and Josh D’Amaro joined Trump and Pat McAfee at Patriot Games
description: Typically, two of the most powerful media executives in the country and the President of the United States wouldn’t be gathered together in Geneva, Ohio on a normal Tuesday in August. But they were this week, thanks to the inaugural Patriot Games. For the uninitiated, the Patriot Games are the brainchild of President Donald Trump…
fullText:
Typically, two of the most powerful media executives in the country and the President of the United States wouldn't be gathered together in Geneva, Ohio on a normal Tuesday in August. But they were this week, thanks to the inaugural Patriot Games.

For the uninitiated, the Patriot Games are the brainchild of President Donald Trump to celebrate America's 250th anniversary. Two high school athletes from each of the 50 states (supposedly), one male and one female, were selected to participate in activities like tug-of-war, pop-a-shot, dodgeball, and kickball. The top 32 athletes advanced to Tuesday's final, in which we already knew Trump and his honored guest Pat McAfee were in attendance.

Now, with the help of some joyous selfies McAfee posted to social media, we also know that there were two key media executives joining him and Trump on Tuesday evening. Both Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro and ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro descended on the small Ohio town, population 5,924, to take in the games.

Had a BLAST celebrating high schoolers from across the country with the Heads of Disney, ABC, ESPN, and… The United States Of America

I’m proud of all parties getting behind this important initiative to keep future generations excited about remaining active.

Cheers to the… pic.twitter.com/FcaLih39qV

— Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) August 12, 2026

The Patriot Games streamed on ESPN's app throughout the past several days, though the competition has received almost no promotion on the Worldwide Leader's air. Laura Rutledge did a quick promo on ABC's Good Morning America over the weekend, but the Games have otherwise been largely ignored on the four-letter network. The only mentions of the Patriot Games have come during McAfee's show, which is not produced by ESPN. Outside of those two hours, ESPN has not mentioned the Patriot Games once.

The network will, however, air a one-hour primetime special of the Patriot Games on Thursday, the lone bit of this circus act that will seep through for public consumption.

The implication is pretty clear. ESPN has tepid interest in the Patriot Games given it's not known property, and most people don't even know of its existence. There are larger priorities to promote for the network. But despite this, Pitaro and D'Amaro show up in an effort to ingratiate themselves with the president. Why else would this duo show up to watch a farcical sporting event in the middle of Ohio that won't even air live on ESPN and that the network refuses to promote? Pitaro probably doesn't even show up to NBA games before the Conference Finals! Now he's showing up to a competition that resembles middle school PE activities? Apparently, that's the cost of doing business under the Trump administration.

Disney has already learned its lesson the hard way. It settled a bogus lawsuit with the Trump administration after ABC News anchor George Stephanopoulos mischaracterized Trump's prior sexual misconduct charges in a minor way, awarding the president's future presidential library $15 million and throwing in an additional $1 million to cover his legal fees.

It's unlikely Pitaro and D'Amaro wanted to be there, or deemed the event important enough for them to attend, aside from the overt political capital gained. But hey, the minor humiliation of legitimizing this weird-ass "sporting event" is worth staying on Trump's good side. Maybe we're being overly cynical and the Patriot Games becomes a regular event with Disney elevating it to a mainstay of the sporting calendar. But either way, as many have learned throughout his decade in public office, Trump's good side is really only available for temporary stays.

title: Trump looms over blue state primary as progressive gov faces far-left challenge
description: Connecticut Democratic Gov. Ned Lamont faces Josh Elliott, who says the incumbent is too "nice" to Trump and calls that a liability against fascism.
fullText:
Connecticut Democratic Gov. Ned Lamont is no fan of President Donald Trump, but his progressive primary challenger, state Rep. Josh Elliott, says he's too cozy with the president.

Lamont defeated Elliott in a high-stakes New England primary Tuesday in a state that not long ago shifted from competitive territory to reliably Democratic.

Elliott, D-Hamden, painted Lamont as too "nice" to Trump, saying that being "nice is a problem right now."

"Nice doesn't solve affordability. Nice doesn't solve fascism or fight back against fascism," Elliott told the Connecticut Mirror.

Anti-trump Senator Defeated By Far-left Rival After Heated Gubernatorial Primary

"[Ned] can be nice all day long, but that's a liability right now."

Lamont, meanwhile, told the outlet that "talk is cheap" and said Elliott has little to offer compared with the incumbent's record during his nearly eight years in office.

Lamont's camp said it wants to see single-payer healthcare and additional resources for early childhood education in the state. Connecticut is increasingly becoming a bedroom community for the New York City, Providence and Boston metropolitan areas.

Gop Gubernatorial Candidate Fighting To Flip Blue State Unveils Healthcare Plan To Lower Costs, Expand Access

Lamont faces state Sen. Ryan Fazio, R-Greenwich, in the November general election.

While now reliably blue, Connecticut not long ago had several Republicans in Congress and GOP governors with staying power, including John Rowland, who was later imprisoned.

Republicans held Connecticut's governorship for much of the period between the Reagan era and 2010, when the late Gov. M. Jodi Rell decided against seeking another term and Democrat Dannel Malloy succeeded her.

Former Sen. Prescott Bush, father of former President George H.W. Bush, represented Connecticut in the U.S. Senate for more than a decade in the mid-20th century.

Lowell Weicker, a liberal Republican U.S. senator who preceded Joseph Lieberman, also served as governor in the 1990s under the "A Connecticut Party" line, which he founded.

title: Trump-backed Mike Lindell refuses to concede Minnesota election loss
description: Mike Lindell, known as the "My Pillow Guy," said he wouldn't concede his primary loss until all the votes are counted. They're now all counted.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — Mike Lindell, a close ally of President Donald Trump known as the "My Pillow Guy," said he's not ready to concede in the Republican primary for Minnesota governor, and blamed potential voting irregularities despite losing by 11 percentage points to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth.

Even as it became clear he would fall short, the Trump-endorsed Lindell told reporters late Tuesday night that he believed 265,000 votes cast on Election Day hadn't been counted and could push him to the lead.

Asked on Aug. 11 whether he would concede if the Associated Press calls the race for his opponent, Lindell said he would not.

"The AP? Why would I listen to the AP?" Lindell said. "There's 265,000 votes left to count. I'm down by 18,000 now. We just gained 5,000. I'm not going to give up this race until the votes are counted. That's nonsense."

Lindell never pulled ahead, and the Associated Press called the election at 11:26 p.m.

More: Election results: Former MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell defeated in GOP primary

Lindell later told reporters he needed time to review the results, convinced the numbers didn't add up correctly based on the final batch of votes. He questioned Minnesota's computerized counting system, and said that all elections should be conducted by paper ballot.

"It just doesn't make sense, you guys. So we need a day. We're going to look into it," Lindell said, suggesting that there could have been voting irregularities, though not specifying what they were. "We've got different teams right now. I've been on the phone with three of them. And the one person said, 'Y, we've seen a couple of anomalies.'"

The Lindell campaign did not respond to an email from USA TODAY asking whether he's still refusing to concede his loss. Lindell has not made any additional public statements since his primary defeat.

More: Mike Lindell steps down as MyPillow CEO to focus on Minnesota campaign

Lindell, who stepped down as CEO of My Pillow to run for governor, has a history of denying election results and remains one of Trump's top defenders backing unfounded claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from Trump.

As Lindell watched a momentary shift in election returns going his way, he expressed confidence that he would overtake Demuth.

"If this is a sign, we will have the lead within an hour," Lindell said. "I mean, this is big news. This is a big jump. They must have started counting the day-of votes."

Lindell didn't get the bounce he needed, however, and Demuth secured the Republican nomination by double digits.

title: Trump administration bans the use of federal Medicaid funds to cover gender identity healthcare
description: The Trump administration on Tuesday finalized a rule that will bar Medicaid from covering gender identity healthcare for children enrolled in the government’s low-income insurance program.
fullText:
The Trump administration on Tuesday finalized a rule that will bar Medicaid from covering gender identity healthcare for children enrolled in the government's low-income insurance program.

The new policy prohibits states from using federal Medicaid funds to pay for any gender identity care for enrollees under 18, marking the administration's latest effort to restrict youth access to transgender healthcare.

President Donald Trump celebrated the move in a Truth Social post, touting it as necessary to crack down on "barbaric surgeries and practices, which result in unthinkable and irreversible harm to their young bodies."

"Just think about all the young, innocent, and perhaps confused children who will be spared!" Trump wrote on social media.

The president has sought to make transgender care a central issue in the run-up to the midterms, frequently describing such gender identity healthcare procedures in graphic terms and claiming, without evidence, that swaths of children are being pressured to secretly transition without their parents' knowledge.

Democrats and a broad range of medical organizations have denounced the Trump administration's efforts to restrict transgender healthcare procedures as harmful and counterproductive, warning that it will further jeopardize children's health.

The administration last year floated the potential for a wider effort to restrict gender identity healthcare for children, including withholding federal funds from hospitals and doctors that continue to offer the procedures.

But the rule finalized Tuesday by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services instead targets coverage provided to low-income enrollees that is funded in part by the federal government.

Under the new policy, states that continue to provide transgender care through Medicaid and CHIP would need to finance it themselves, without the aid of federal money that helps pay for a significant share of the insurance programs. In a statement, CMS said that the funding ban would not apply to mental health services for children.

The rule is set to take effect on October 13, according to CMS. For those children who are currently receiving gender identity care, federal funds will remain available for six months to allow for a "tapering off" period.

title: Trump's approval rating hits yet another record low in latest poll
description: President Trump’s approval rating has fallen to yet another low for his second term in the White House, according to a new Economist/YouGov poll.
fullText:
President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to yet another low since his return to the White House, according to a new Economist/YouGov poll, which also found that just 1 in 3 Americans approve of his job performance.

The survey, released Aug. 11, found that 33% of Americans approve of Trump's performance, down 3 percentage points from the previous week. This marks the lowest approval rating the president has seen in YouGov tracking since he returned to office in 2025.

Apart from his continued slump in the polls, a majority of Americans, 60%, said they perceived the president as "not honest and trustworthy". According to the newest poll, 65% of respondents said the country is headed in the wrong direction, up 2 percentage points from the Economist/YouGov's poll in late July.

The latest poll also found that Trump's age continues to concern the American public, with 53% saying they believed the 80-year-old president was too old to be in the White House.

The Economist/YouGov poll was conducted Aug. 7-10 among 1,589 U.S. adults. The poll's margin of error was plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

Trump's slide in the polls in recent weeks could signify good news for Democrats ahead of November's midterm elections. In the newest Economist/YouGov poll, Democrats hold an 8-point lead over the GOP in a generic congressional ballot.

That lead has held in other surveys, as a poll released by Marquette Law School on Aug. 5 showed Democrats holding a 6-point advantage over Republicans. Another survey released Aug. 3 by Reuters/Ipsos had the Democratic Party holding a 5-point lead over the GOP.

Last week, Trump said the Republican base is angry at the party's leadership in Congress, not him, ahead of the midterms.

"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in an interview with Punchbowl News. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

The president's remarks came as he dismissed his current approval ratings by defending his popularity, specifically pointing to his 2024 election wins in several states.

"I have records in many of the states," Trump said. "The question is ... if I don't run, will those people go out and vote? And that's the one thing I can't tell you. I'm going to ask them to."

Aside from Trump's continued struggles with his approval rating, a majority of respondents in the newest poll also said they believed the president is using his presidential powers for his own benefit.

According to the Economist/YouGov poll, 61% of respondents said they believed Trump was using his office for personal gain, and 55% said they believed the president was using the Department of Justice to go after his political enemies.

Trump's controversial East Wing ballroom in the White House has also remained unpopular with Americans, with 57% saying they oppose it.

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Aug. 11): 39.2% approve, 58.6% disapprove

New York Times (Aug. 11): 37% approve, 59% disapprove

Silver Bulletin (Aug. 11): 38.1% approve, 58.5% disapprove

USA TODAY's Kinsey Crowley contributed to this report.

title: Sherrill drops head-turning voter ID declaration in wake of registration fiasco: ‘Significant shift’
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill says she would support voter ID in New Jersey, even as she blasts the federal SAVE Act that Donald Trump champions as suppression.
fullText:
New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill says she would support a voter ID law in the Garden State — even as she slams President Donald Trump's federal SAVE Act push as "voter suppression."

"Governor Sherrill supports the current rules requiring ID for voter registration and she is open to considering proposals to strengthen those to make sure we have the strongest, fairest elections in the nation," a spokesperson in the governor's office told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

Sherrill's comments hand New Jersey Republicans a new opening to press Democrats on voter ID, even as she rejects Trump's broader federal election push under the SAVE America Act.

Sherrill's office responded to Fox News Digital on Tuesday after the Garden State Democrat told local media in July she would support a voter ID law if one were passed in New Jersey, saying she "doesn't have a problem with voter ID."

Schumer Said 'Democrats Support Voter Id' — Then Every Senate Democrat Voted Against Gop Bill

"I'm very opposed to the SAVE Act," Sherrill added at the time. "I do believe that is just a tool of voter suppression and an attempt to get all of the personal identifying information of New Jerseyans into the federal government systems, which I'm opposed to."

Sherrill served in the House for seven years and voted against the SAVE Act in 2025, with her office describing the measure as an "extreme voter suppression bill."

Sherrill is facing criticism after announcing last month that a Motor Vehicle Commission system error improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who had indicated they were not U.S. citizens. The state said fewer than 400 people newly registered because of the error voted, and later announced that more than 4,500 registrations were being removed while the remaining cases undergo additional review because some of those individuals may be citizens.

New Jersey Assembly Minority Leader John DiMaio told Fox News Digital Sherrill's recent comments mark a "significant shift" after years of Republicans in the Garden State advocating for voter ID.

New Jersey Removes 6,600 People From Voter Rolls Who Were Eligible To Cast A Ballot For 2024 Election

"But agreeing with us publicly is the easy part," DiMaio said, adding that Democratic legislative leaders control what gets a hearing and a vote, and that Republicans have so far heard nothing from them on voter ID.

"We've been pushing voter ID and other election integrity reforms for years. The bills are already introduced. We've repeatedly called for hearings and votes. The roadblock has been Democratic legislative leadership," the Republican state leader said.

DiMaio said the Motor Vehicle System failure exposed serious weaknesses in New Jersey's election safeguards and they still have not heard an answer of what went wrong.

Voter-ID requirements have repeatedly become major partisan fights at the state level, with Democrats and voting-rights groups arguing that some requirements can make it harder for eligible voters to cast ballots.

One of the most prominent battles erupted in Georgia in 2021. The state already required photo ID for in-person voting, but a sweeping Republican-backed election law added identification requirements for absentee voting along with other changes. The backlash went national, with MLB moving its 2021 All-Star Game out of Atlanta and some Hollywood figures threatening boycotts.

Harris Becomes Accidental Save Act 'Saleswoman' As Trump Attack Spectacularly Backfires

"Governor Sherrill served our country in the military and as a public servant because she believes in every citizen's right to participate in our democracy by voting. That's why she has stood firm against MAGA Republicans' voter suppression attempts and Trump's demands for New Jersey voters' personal identifiable information," said a spokesperson in the office of the governor.

"She has already made voting more accessible by signing the John R. Lewis Voter Empowerment Act and expanded early voting in municipal elections," the spokesperson added, referencing the law that bans voter intimidation and discrimination, expanding language assistance, and requiring extra review of election changes in places with a history of discrimination.

Trump has continued to prioritize and highlight the issue of noncitizens on voter rolls as he renewed his push for the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register for federal elections and photo identification to cast a federal ballot.

"I think they should pass Voter I.D. I think they should pass proof of citizenship—basically SAVE America Act... I think that should be something that we should absolutely get," Trump said in the Oval Office Monday.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

title: Trump lashes out after liberal think tank says National Guard deployments did not reduce violent crime
description: President Trump on Monday lashed out at the Center for American Progress (CAP), a liberal think tank, after it released a report last month suggesting the National Guard deployments failed to reduce v...
fullText:
President Trump on Monday lashed out at the Center for American Progress (CAP), a liberal think tank, after it released a report last month suggesting the National Guard deployments failed to reduce violent crime.

"Chandler Hall, representing, on Television, the foolish Center for American Lack of Progress, stated that adding the National Guard to Cities, including our now Great Again, Washington, D.C., had 'NO impact on Crime,'" Trump wrote on Truth Social, referring to the report's author. "How crazy is that. Hall was met with furious dissent."

Trump called the research "another Radical Left SCAM, as are the people who fund this gaggle of Lunatics, including George Soros, Bill and Melinda Gates, Google, Apple, Visa, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, Walmart, Toyota, T-Mobile, and NBC Universal."

He added that he will file a lawsuit and add "some of the contributors to this Fake Organization."

"Crime is way down since I took Office, and they know it," the president concluded. "Liars, at this level, must be held accountable!"

Chandler Hall, CAP's associate director of public safety, appeared on C-SPAN's "Washington Journal" on Monday to talk about the July report, titled "The Trump Administration's $1.7 Billion National Guard Deployments Fail To Reduce Urban Crime."

His findings suggest that the deployments have not reduced violent crime, as incidents were already trending downward well before Trump deployed the National Guard to various cities.

"What we find is that across multiple cities, multiple datasets, and multiple time windows, we find no effect that violent crime actually did change post the National Guard deployment in any of the cities," Hall said, later noting that there is a lack of "consistent data infrastructure" when tabulating what constitutes violent crime in different American cities.

He was faced with questions around Trump's recent remarks to reporters about the crime rate in the nation's capital, saying the District went from being the "crime capital, frankly, in the world" to "one of the safest places in the United States."

The CAP author said that violent crime and homicides decreased in Washington even before the COVID-19 pandemic, thus predating Trump's National Guard deployment. He added that it was "quite evident" that there is still crime in the city despite the president's claim that it's among the safest.

"I think it's unfortunate that the president is continuing to still choose to boast that these deployments, these very costly interventions, are showing any results to try to convince voters that they should sign on for more of these kind of interventions in federal overreach, when, again, there's no proof that they have any effect," Hall said on C-SPAN. "And, in fact, it actually is making it more difficult for the work that's already been done in the city."

He also noted toward the end of the report that, based on the findings, the deployments "effectuated a dangerous power grab by the Trump administration" and "increased unrest in the cities that felt their independence being threatened."

The Major Cities Chiefs Association's own report, which breaks down crime statistics from January through the end of June this year, found crime rates declining across the board, with homicides down just more than 17 percent and robberies down more than 16 percent.

The Washington Post reported last week that the Pentagon's deployment of the National Guard in Washington is projected to cost another $1.4 billion through the end of Trump's term in 2029.

title: US allies say they’re worried about Trump’s clout after Netanyahu rejected deal
description: Diplomats say they’re worried the Trump administration’s negotiating efforts in Israel can’t recover.
fullText:
U.S. allies see Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Washington's 15-point plan for Gaza as undermining confidence in the Board of Peace — and in the Trump administration's ability to influence the Middle East more broadly.

It increasingly appears that the U.S. either doesn't have — or isn't willing to exercise — the leverage needed to deliver on Gaza, a number of diplomats and others familiar with U.S. strategy in the region told POLITICO. And that has them concerned about U.S. efforts at negotiations across the region.

"Netanyahu's rejection of the peace plan carries significant implications for long-term regional stability and Israeli security," said an Arab diplomat familiar with U.S. policy in the Middle East. "President Trump is the only one to have the potential to influence this situation, as he could seek to reassert his political relevance by pressuring Netanyahu to reconsider his position."

Netanyahu's defiance adds to the growing list of woes Washington faces as it struggles to reshape the Middle East, from ending the Iran war to winding down the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

The Arab diplomat warned: "Arab and regional leaders may find themselves in a complex position, needing to balance their interests amid these evolving dynamics."

Netanyahu disavowed the White House-backed peace plan for Gaza on Sunday, declaring that Israel requires Hamas to have "genuinely disarmed" before it withdraws its troops from the territory. That hard line could further threaten the viability of Trump's Board of Peace, a 27-country initiative formed as part of Trump's deal last year to end the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

"The Board of Peace has a distinct limp to its gait at the moment," said Robert Jordan, who served as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia during the George W. Bush administration.

"It never appeared to be a broadly based, highly viable substitute for the United Nations," he added, referring to Trump's assertions in January that the board could be used as an alternative to the world body. "That's compounded by the political situation in Israel at the moment."

The Board of Peace declined to comment, but an official with the organization insisted that work is continuing apace, with Israel's buy-in. The official pointed to a logistical support area under construction that is meant to serve hundreds of troops expected to deploy to Gaza as part of the international stabilization force envisioned by the board.

"The roadmap is between the Board of Peace and Hamas," said the board official. "Separate discussions with Israel are continuing. Israel is not being asked to rely on trust or to make irreversible moves before verified steps are taken on the ground."

The official, like others, was granted anonymity because of the sensitivity of the negotiation process.

A Western diplomat familiar with Middle East policy argued Netanyahu's action is a sign that U.S. strategy toward Israel is misguided.

"This latest rejection once again shows that appeasing Israel only leads to more maximalist demands," the diplomat said. "I don't think it kills the [Board of Peace] but what it does do is once again show that Israel remains one of the obstacles to a viable two-state solution."

Trump has avoided clashing publicly with Netanyahu over the roadmap, telling reporters Monday that he had a "good relationship" with the Israeli prime minister even though Netanyahu rejected the U.S. proposal. The White House declined to comment further on Israel's rejection of the deal.

A Trump administration official, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the issue publicly, said the White House doesn't see Netanyahu's action as derailing the peace process at all.

"Broadly speaking, we see this as election-posturing by Bibi for a domestic audience," the official said. "The [Board of Peace] has actually been getting good cooperation on the ground as of late. So that's what's important."

Netanyahu's rejection of the road map comes as his popularity has been eroding in Israel ahead of an October parliamentary vote that could lead to his unseating.

In Europe, some governments are still holding out hope that the Board of Peace can rescue the Gaza peace process.

"I extremely appreciate the work of chief negotiator [Nickolay] Mladenov on behalf of the Board of Peace, his achievements in the 15-point plan are absolutely substantial," said Hildegard Bentele, a center-right German lawmaker in the European Parliament. He said he was confident the U.S.-led effort would make progress "if re-submitted after Israeli elections and targeting the core point of full weapons' decommissioning."

Others with experience in the region said that Netanyahu appeared to be successfully pushing the Board of Peace in a direction more favorable to Israel.

Netanyahu's actions are "testing the tolerance of the American or Board of Peace team," said Nimrod Novik, who served as senior diplomatic adviser to former Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres and is now a fellow at the New York-based Israel Policy Forum.

"It's really a Trump personal enterprise," said Zaha Hassan, who advised the Palestinian negotiating team during its bid for U.N. membership from 2010 to 2012 and is now a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. "So if it can't get Israel to stand down in Gaza, to withdraw, to allow the Board of Peace to do its work, how can any other regional actor believe that the U.S. can restrain Israel in their neighborhood?"

A European diplomat said the disillusionment with Trump's sway in the Middle East was already evident in his failure to wrap up the war in Iran quickly.

"The solution is not as close as anticipated or as Trump told us at some point. I think Trump is losing credibility," said the diplomat, granted anonymity because they weren't authorized to discuss the issue publicly. "Everything seems to be in limbo and in a high degree of uncertainty that affects us all."

Aug 11 (Reuters) - The Trump administration on Tuesday finalized a rule exempting U.S. companies and individuals from ‌reporting beneficial ownership information to the Treasury Department's financial ‌crimes unit, rolling back reporting requirements established under a 2021 law aimed ​at combating illicit finance.

The Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, will still require foreign reporting companies to disclose beneficial ownership information for foreign individuals, the department said in a ‌statement.

"Treasury is eliminating a ⁠burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security," Treasury ⁠Secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement.

Beneficial owners are defined as anyone who has an ownership interest of at least 25% ​in a ​business or someone who exerts "substantial ​control" over the entity.

FinCEN ‌had previously implemented rules requiring certain companies to report beneficial ownership data as part of anti-corruption and anti-money laundering efforts backed by lawmakers and the Treasury Department under former President Joe Biden.

The Treasury Department said that FinCEN will delete previously ‌reported information by Americans from the ​government's beneficial ownership information database.

Under the ​rule finalized on Tuesday, ​foreign companies would not be required to ‌report Americans who helped those foreign ​companies register ​to do business in the United States.

It also exempts foreign pooled investment vehicles registered in the United States from ​reporting the beneficial ‌ownership information of a U.S person in control of ​the investment vehicle, the Treasury Department said.

title: Trump doesn't dismiss declaring national emergency to restrict voting
description: "Stranger things have happened," Trump said when an interviewer suggested he declare a national emergency to take executive action on voting.
fullText:
President Donald Trump isn't dismissing the possibility that he could declare a national security emergency in an attempt to establish new voting restrictions stalled in the Senate, telling an interviewer that "stranger things have happened."

Trump has spent weeks hammering senators to pass the SAVE America Act, legislation that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and a photo ID when casting a ballot.

The bill is Trump's top legislative priority, but it has struggled to attract enough support in the Senate, and lawmakers left for their August recess last week without passing it.

During a Real America's Voice interview with Trump on Aug. 10, host Wayne Allyn Root suggested declaring a national emergency to implement voting changes, a move that almost certainly would be challenged in court.

"Let me put an idea in your head, OK?" Root said, adding: "If they never get the SAVE America Act done, you have the right to declare a national security emergency for elections … so if you do this in the next month we will get photo ID, proof of citizenship and a limit to mail-in ballots and you don't even need the Senate's vote."

"Let me just say that stranger things have happened, OK?" Trump interjected. "I'll leave it at that."

The comments come as Trump has taken steps to assert greater federal authority over elections, which are administered by state and local officials. Trump suggested earlier this year that Republicans should "nationalize" the voting process, generating bipartisan pushback and alarming opponents who worried about the fairness of future contests.

"Donald Trump wants to take over American elections," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, said in response to Trump's remarks to Root.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The president issued an executive order in March that moved to exert federal control over voter rolls and mail-in ballots. Trump directed the Department of Homeland Security to develop lists of eligible voters in each state and ordered the U.S. Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on the approved lists.

The move escalated Trump's bid to place new restrictions on voting ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake. It was quickly challenged in court by Democrat-led states, and on June 25 a federal judge in Boston blocked the order.

The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court on July 27 seeking permission to implement two provisions in the order. The states that brought the lawsuit responded in a court filing that there would be "extraordinary consequences" from allowing the order to proceed.

Trump has argued that new voting rules are needed to safeguard elections as he makes unfounded claims about widespread voter fraud. Democrats and voting rights groups say the SAVE America Act would disenfranchise millions of eligible voters.

title: Opinion - The Blanche appointment is another Trump win that’s America’s loss
description: He will serve only Donald Trump, not our precious rule of law.
fullText:
Trump ballyhooed the appointment of Todd Blanche to become the nation's 88th attorney general with the exaggerated claim, "Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it!"

It is to the shame of the U.S. Senate that Blanche is now confirmed. It is the worst appointment of the second Trump administration. Yes, you heard me — worse than Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard or Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem put together, because he will serve only President Trump, not our precious rule of law.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who cast the deciding vote, said in an absurd statement that Blanche "is not perfect … but the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche," it is "between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who … may not be as good as Mr. Blanche."

Blanche has proved himself a petty bureaucrat jumping at Trump's call; a lawyer of distinction he is not.

Ask the more than 1,200 of Blanche's Department of Justice colleagues who urged the Senate to reject his nomination. Ask the 35 former federal judges from across the country who have argued he committed a fraud on the court. Incumbent federal judges have said that the Justice Department under his aegis is no longer entitled to the presumption of regularity. He has lied to the courts once too often. In July, a judge forced Blanche's prosecutors to withdraw subpoenas served on New York Times reporters at their homes, finding serious irregularities.

Under Blanche, grand juries have refused to return indictments. The government reportedly could not persuade a single grand juror to sign off on proposed criminal charges against six Democratic lawmakers who released a video encouraging members of the military to refuse illegal orders. A grand jury refused to indict a man for assault who threw a sandwich at a federal agent.

It's not that he lost. It's about what kind of attorney general prosecutes cases like this. Where is the judgment?

Blanche tried to install Lindsey Halligan as the U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia to mount a vindictive case against Trump's enemy, former F.B.I. director James Comey. But judges, finding she had been improperly appointed, dismissed the case against Comey, as well as a separate one Halligan tried to bring against New York Attorney General Letitia James. Comey later moved to dismiss a ridiculous second indictment, in which he was charged with photographing an arrangement of seashells on a beach.

Before leaving the Justice Department, Halligan kept using the U.S. attorney title, despite the court's ruling. Blanche defended her actions in a response that displayed, as a presiding judge put it, "a level of vitriol more appropriate for a cable news talk show."

Under Blanche, the Justice Department has suffered a flight of career attorneys. Seasoned lawyers who worked on Trump prosecutions have been fired. Others have flocked for the exits, finding that politicized prosecutions are inconsistent with principled governmental service.

The 50 Senate Republican votes to confirm Blanche came after his appointment was nearly derailed when Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) threatened to vote against him over the deal he struck this spring to resolve Trump's questionable legal claims against the IRS.

They wanted written assurances that the Justice Department would not move forward with aspects of the settlement, including a proposed $1.8 billion slush fund for people like the Jan. 6 insurrectionists who claimed they were victims of "politicized" prosecutions under Obama and Biden. The slush fund was the kettle calling the pot black.

Both senators said that Blanche had allayed their concerns in statements issued last Sunday purporting to impose limits on the deal. The statements were worthless. As Tillis switched his vote in favor of Blanche, he seemed to acknowledge that they could be reversed by the president.

Several GOP lawmakers said they were somewhat reassured by the "concessions" Tillis and Cornyn had extracted from Blanche. Strange because even if the anti-weaponization fund isn't revived, Trump can still make payouts to allies through individual settlements. Blanche has also essentially left in place the deal that shields the president, his sons and their businesses from past tax claims. The release is said to be worth $600 million.

"There is enough weasel room in these documents to drive a truck through," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.).

Then, there is the elephant in the room: the Epstein files, with the drip-feed, heavily redacted disclosure Blanche handled, not to mention his callous mistreatment of Epstein's victims. A New York Times report by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan exposed that Blanche handled the Epstein case as a matter of politics, and key decisions were made by Blanche in collaboration with the White House.

In 1940, Attorney General Robert Jackson declared in the prosecutor's creed that, "the citizen's safety lies in the prosecutor who tempers zeal with human kindness, who seeks truth and not victims, who serves the law and not factional purposes, and who approaches his task with humility."

Blanche has been confirmed to serve "factional purposes." If he is not "perfect," he should not have been confirmed.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

title: GOP senators rally behind Thune in response to Trump jabs at leader
description: Senate Republicans are rallying behind Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) after President Trump declined to support the GOP leader serving another term following the midterm election. Many Rep...
fullText:
Senate Republicans are rallying behind Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) after President Trump declined to support the GOP leader serving another term following the midterm election.

Many Republican senators say Thune will have their full support, even if Trump backs a challenger, because of the Senate leader's refusal to abolish the filibuster to advance Trump's top legislative priorities, such as the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

"There's a lot of respect for John Thune. There's a lot of recognition of how he works and how difficult his job is and a belief that he's doing it really well under difficult circumstances," said Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).

Moran said Republican senators have been willing to yield to the president on a lot of issues but that they would draw a line against letting Trump push Thune out of his job or pick a replacement.

"I also think there are some things where the Senate seems willing to accede their privileges, but I think who our leader is, there's a real sense that that belongs to us," he said.

Even Senate conservatives who have ratcheted up pressure on Thune to keep the upper chamber in session during the August recess to debate the SAVE America Act acknowledge that Thune has had to navigate a political minefield as GOP leader.

"It's a hard job, it's really a hard job," said Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a leading proponent of the SAVE America Act.

Asked if he continues to have confidence in Thune despite the growing criticism from the White House, Scott noted that presidents often get frustrated with the Senate's 60-vote hurdle to passing their legislative priorities.

"I'm sure if I were president of the United States, I would be frustrated if everything I wanted didn't get done. So that's probably pretty common," the Florida senator said.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said he's doesn't "know of any movements to replace" Thune even though Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration over his agenda getting bogged down in the Senate.

"I think the president and John like each other. I think these are tough issues and they obviously disagree over things like the filibuster," Kennedy said.

Trump last week insisted in an interview with Punchbowl News that Republican voters are "not angry at me, but they are angry at Republicans" in Congress.

But even Trump's allies on Capitol Hill aren't buying that claim.

"I think Republicans are angry at all of us, I mean the voters. I think the voters are angry, period. And I think they're angry most about … cost of living, and I think that's what this election is going to be primarily about," Kennedy said.

"One of the reasons that the democratic socialists are winning elections is because they stand for something. Now what they stand for sucks, but a lot of their support is coming from young people who don't know history," the Louisiana senator continued.

GOP lawmakers think Trump has caused political headwinds for their party by not being more attuned to the affordability crisis, which Trump downplayed as a "hoax" issue driven by Democrats.

And while Trump has traveled around the country to talk about his economic accomplishments, he is prone to veering away from his script to hit on hot-button political issues, such as calls to pass the SAVE America Act to avert fraud in the upcoming election.

Thune has tried to shrug off Trump's criticisms in recent weeks, but they're becoming tougher to downplay as the president continues to suggest that the Senate GOP leader isn't getting his job done and that voters aren't happy with Republicans in Congress as a result.

Thune said he almost "expected" Trump to withhold his endorsement for him serving another term as Senate leader.

"That's probably to be expected," Thune said with a trace of resignation in his voice.

And Thune argued just as the Senate was leaving that his Republican colleagues have done a lot of heavy lifting to get the president's agenda passed, disputing Trump's accusations that they're not doing their jobs.

Thune said he and other Senate Republicans feel they are getting a lot done for Trump.

"I think we've had a really productive run. There are a couple things I said right from the very beginning are going to be difficult if not impossible — frankly more impossible — to do," he said of Trump's calls to pass the SAVE America Act and abolish the filibuster.

"That's the reality I have to deal with," Thune said of Democratic opposition to voting reforms and Republican opposition to lowering the threshold for passing legislation from 60 votes to a simple majority.

The GOP leader said the president is "entitled to his views," and Thune is "fine with that," but he argued getting Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed despite strong reservations from a handful of GOP senators, coupled with the prolonged absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), was a "good, solid win for the team and obviously … not an easy one."

"We'll keep grinding away and let the chips fall where they may," Thune added.

One Thune ally said Trump's public criticism of the Senate leader is a tactic he is using to put "pressure" on Thune to pass as much of the president's agenda as possible and predicted it could "change" after the election.

Even so, Trump's refusal to say whether Thune is "still the man for the job" — coupled with White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt's statement that Trump's "patience is running out" with Thune's job performance — has fueled the appearance that their personal relationship is on shaky ground.

Thune has winced or hinted at his frustration at times when asked about the latest rumble of dissatisfaction from Trump but has mainly stayed focused on enacting as much of his agenda as possible before Democrats have a chance to win back control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Yet a growing number of Senate Republicans see Trump and his low approval ratings — especially on the economy — as a bigger political problem than strategic decisions made by Thune and his leadership team.

GOP lawmakers are seeking to distance themselves from Trump ahead of the November election as polls show independent voters moving away from the president and Republican voters losing enthusiasm for him.

More than half the Senate GOP conference pushed back against the Justice Department's proposal to establish a nearly $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund for Trump's MAGA allies at a fiery meeting with Blanche in May.

GOP senators also quashed Trump's push for $1 billion in funding for the new 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom and are now currently resisting his call for immediate passage of a budget resolution to fund the unpopular military conflict with Iran.

A group of Senate Republicans last week bristled over the White House intervening in a stopgap spending bill to fund the government until Dec. 11 by adding language to delay the implementation of a ban on hemp-derived THC products — a policy rider that deeply divided their conference.

One GOP senator fumed the move was "not rational," given the uproar it created within the conference, to delay the implementation of the ban by only a month.

"I don't understand why this is an issue. What's the heartburn over just a few weeks? They say there's someone very close to the White House who has an interest in this," the lawmaker added, referring to media reports that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles's son-in-law, Bret Worley, is the CEO of companies that make hemp-derived intoxicating gummies and vapes.

GOP senators vented their complaints over the hemp-products rider to White House staff during a closed-door meeting but later acceded to the White House's will on the issue by voting early Saturday morning to table an amendment sponsored by Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) to strip the White House-backed hemp language from the government funding stopgap.

"This issue has got everybody in the conference spun up," the senator added. "If the president were to veto a CR [continuing resolution] over this? Wow. But that's kind of the worry."

title: Russia frees ailing ex-US Marine Robert Gilman from detention
description: Russia on Tuesday freed a former American Marine who had been jailed in the country since 2022, U. In a social media post, Trump said Russia agreed to release Robert Gil...
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Russia on Tuesday freed a former American Marine who had been jailed in the country since 2022, U.S. President Donald Trump said.

In a social media post, Trump said Russia agreed to release Robert Gilman, 32, for humanitarian ‌reasons after discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin, adding that the ailing American would arrive at Joint Base Andrews near Washington on Tuesday night.

"I am ‌proud to announce that American Citizen Robert Gilman, a former United States Marine, is coming HOME!" Trump said. "We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange ​took place."

The White House and the State Department had urged Moscow to release Gilman so he could receive medical treatment in the United States. U.S. officials said Putin approved a pardon for him.

Gilman was being held in a prison in Voronezh, about 340 miles (550 kilometers) south of Moscow. The exact circumstances of his health are unclear.

But Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of Global Reach, an advocacy group representing Gilman's family, told Reuters last week that Gilman was moved in late June from the prison hospital to the psychiatric ward ‌of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state assessed ⁠as a "dissociative stupor."

A U.S. official who spoke to Gilman said he was walking and talking.

"All things considered he seems to be in good shape," the official said.

Trump's post included a photo of a gaunt-looking man on a plane surrounded by a group of ⁠smiling people carrying an American flag. The president said he had spoken to Gilman, who requested a cheeseburger upon landing.

"I will take care of that!" Trump said.

Gilman will be evaluated on the flight by four doctors, said the U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

After that, Gilman is likely to be flown to a rehabilitation center in San Antonio, Texas, for ​medical ​treatment, the officials said.

ARRESTED OVER POLICE OFFICER INCIDENT

Gilman, who served in the U.S. Marines from August ​2019 until August 2020, was traveling by train when he was ‌arrested in January 2022 in Voronezh, Lebson said.

He was detained for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media.

However, his father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that the charges were false.

His son, he said, had fallen ill when the incident occurred and accidentally kicked the officer. The officer was uninjured, dropped the charges, and did not present evidence at Gilman's trial, he wrote.

Robert Gilman was sentenced to 4-1/2 years in jail. He was one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in Russia.

The U.S. officials said a Russian senior official, Yuri Ushakov, informed Trump aides ‌last week that Putin had agreed to sign a decree pardoning Gilman for humanitarian purposes, given ​Putin's friendship with the president.

The release resulted from intense negotiations over the weekend by U.S. and ​Russian officials. The U.S. did not exchange any Russian prisoners in order to ​gain Gilman's release and no concessions were made, the officials said.

"It's a goodwill gesture," one official said.

Trump thanked U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, ‌senior director for counterterrorism Sebastian Gorka, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, ​and U.S. special envoy for hostage response Adam ​Boehler for making the release possible.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Gilman is among 100 U.S. citizens whose freedom Trump has helped secure during his second term in office. Rubio said the U.S. appreciated the "positive step," but called for the release of other Americans who he said were unjustly ​detained in Russia, including Stephen Hubbard.

Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher, was ‌sentenced in October 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony after a court found him guilty of serving in a Ukrainian territorial ​defense unit against Russian forces, tasked with manning a checkpoint.

title: Violent crime up in DC despite Trump boast of National Guard presence
description: Washington DC 2026 crime numbers show varying results from the National Guard deployment, which was ordered by President Donald Trump last year.
fullText:
President Donald Trump said during his State of the Union address in February that Washington DC has "almost no crime anymore" thanks to his deployment of the National Guard last August.

They were comments he took a step further in July, when he said DC has gone to levels of "NO CRIME" under his leadership.

The president is right; overall crime is down in DC. Fueled by a 53% drop in motor vehicle theft and a 37% decrease in theft from automobiles, there has been 23% less property crime in DC from 2026 to 2025, according to police data.

But numbers provided by the Metropolitan Police Department tell a different story, one that shows violent crime numbers are up this year.

Here's a look at the 2026 violent crime numbers in Washington DC and how they compare to 2025, with the National Guard deployment to continue through the entirety of Trump's presidency.

Trump's assertion that crime has been wiped out in DC falls short when compared to DC police statistics.

As of Aug. 10, there were 1,655 reported instances of violent crime in the city — 55 more than the same period from last year.

Most of that increase is due to a sharp upswing in reports of assault with a deadly weapon. There is a 41% increase in such activity, with 767 cases so far this year.

The data does show homicides are down — 67 cases this year, compared to 97 on this date in 2025 — but the summer has seen a dramatic increase.

There have been 32 homicides since the beginning of June, including nine in the past two weeks, police data shows.

While DC's homicide rates have improved, data shows that they're actually down throughout the country.

"It's really hard to parse out any effect of the federal deployment in DC, necessarily, because it is a city that was already seeing really strong declines," Jeff Asher, co-founder of the data analytics firm AH Datalytics, told USA TODAY earlier this year.

From 2024 to 2025 — less than half of which featured the National Guard's deployment — violent crime was down 29% in DC. There were 274 homicides in 2023 and 187 in 2024, and the city saw another decrease last year with 127 homicides.

title: All-powerful Trump tells America, ‘Nothing bad can happen’
description: Trump signed an executive order aimed at reducing the number of childhood vaccines.
fullText:
Just one of the wild actions and comments on Donald Trump's manic Monday would rank among the most notorious things another president ever did.

Often, the round-the-clock cacophony from the White House seems expressly designed to stifle public comprehension of each individual act planned to irrevocably change the country and the world.

This was certainly the case on a day that fulfilled some core goals of the Trump base but also helped to explain the plunging presidential approval ratings that have Republicans looking with dread toward the midterm elections.

It all started when one of the president's former personal lawyers, now Appeals Court Judge Emil Bove, swore in another of the president's former personal lawyers, Todd Blanche, as attorney general.

This was peak Trump. Nine years after the president asked James Comey for loyalty — as the fired former FBI chief told it — one of his ultimate loyalists was on Monday installed in a Senate-confirmed position at the pinnacle of US justice.

Blanche was with Trump in some of his darkest moments as he faced multiple criminal and civil charges before winning back the White House. Some Trump subordinates, like former Attorney General Pam Bondi, stumbled when striving to prove their loyalty. But Blanche has already demonstrated fealty — one reason his critics fear him and wonder whether he'll act a spiritual successor to Trump's McCarthyite lawyer Roy Cohn.

As Blanche was clapped by staff back into his agency, more of the president's men gathered by the Resolute Desk. He was about to act on a feeling he's harbored even longer than his quest to make the DOJ his boutique law firm.

Trump then signed an executive order aimed at reducing the number of childhood vaccines. And he administered a fresh dose of unscientific falsehoods, baselessly claiming vaccines cause autism and that little children had had inoculations the size of soda bottles poured into their bodies. At one point, he suggested that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal" — amid a year when the US has recorded the most measles cases in more than a quarter-century. It was hard not to get flashbacks to his erratic Covid-19 pandemic news conferences.

But America's most powerful public health official and vaccine skeptic, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., insisted: "This is what gold-standard science means."

Trump confirmed he'd recently spoken to new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, but denied a Wall Street Journal report they'd had multiple conversations. The president has left no doubt he wants Warsh to lower interest rates. "If it was up to him, it would be different, but he has a board," Trump said, raising doubts about the central bank's independence.

The president also weighed in on the triumph of progressive and democratic socialist candidates in Democratic primaries ahead of the midterm elections: "We have jihadists being elected all over the place."

The president's latest inflammatory comment about Muslim candidates appears to herald a viciously negative fall campaign. He didn't specify who he was talking about, but his remark came a week after Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary.

When he turned to Iran, the president showed how the once-intricate US foreign policy process has ceded to the wish-casting of the commander in chief who declared a war won after a few days that is now in its sixth month. And he claimed the Strait of Hormuz, an oil exporting choke point effectively controlled by Iran, is "opened now." The Windward Maritime Intelligence Operations Center said Monday that only seven vessels had crossed the strait in the previous 24 hours. Before the war, the waterway often saw more than 100 ships a day.

Each of these examples show how Trump has degraded the institutions of US government and purged them of experts, bureaucrats and officials who don't share his idiosyncratic worldview.

Many Trump supporters argue that he's making good on his vow to dismantle a corrupt administrative state that has long thwarted conservative presidents. Others promote the idea of an all-powerful presidency and 

In some ways, the maelstrom of business across the Oval Office desk Monday mirrors the deeply centralized decision-making process developed for years by the future president at the Trump Organization, where he was the sole source of authority. But Trump's critics see his hands-on style as the behavior of a wannabe authoritarian and argue his hunch-driven style of leadership is a recipe for disaster.

It's hard to make a case that Trump's approach is working for anyone outside his most loyal support base, despite his claim in an interview with Punchbowl News last week that "a lot of people are saying I'm one of the greatest presidents ever."

In a recent CNN/SSRS poll, only 21% of Americans said Trump's military action in Iran had helped the US. Many analysts believe he's led the US into a stalemate against a much weaker nation.

His crusade to dominate the Justice Department is one of the personal fixations — along with his monument-building program — that help explain why a record-high 73% of US adults said in that same CNN survey that he hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems.

And according to polling from the health policy nonprofit KFF, an 81% majority of US adults say they are confident that MMR vaccines are safe for children. A small sector of Trump's base, however, has long bought into the anti-vaccine movement.

Some of the institutionalists who Trump disdains warned on Monday evening that his increasingly unchecked presidency is dangerous.

"It is simply astonishing that this administration would continue to respond to ongoing measles outbreaks and the return of other vaccine-preventable diseases by playing politics with children's lives," said Dr. Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

David Axelrod, who served as a counselor to Barack Obama, told CNN's Erin Burnett that a president's words "can send armies marching and markets tumbling." But they can "also jeopardize people's health because the president has enormous sway. … It's really, really dangerous."

But Trump is beyond listening. Explaining his vaccine policy, he seemed both to encapsulate his attitude to unchecked power and to tempt fate.

"Nothing bad can happen from what we're doing," he said. "Nothing bad can happen."

title: When MAGA met FIFA: Inside Trump’s cosy relationship with Gianni Infantino
description: President Trump has given his full backing to embattled Infantino as the FIFA president faces ongoing pressure to step down
fullText:
President Donald Trump has thrown his weight behind embattled FIFA President Gianni Infantino as the football chief faces ongoing pressure to resign.

The U.S. president warned FIFA that it would be a "terrible mistake" to even consider ousting Infantino, amid widespread backlash over the latter's plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"​

Swiss-born Infantino has been criticized by a slew of organizations and world leaders, including UEFA, Europe's football governing body, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Below we look at the history of Infantino and Trump's relationship as the pair continue to support each other on the world's stage.

Trump and Infantino's relationship can be traced back to 2018, two years after both he and Infantino won their first presidencies.

The commander-in-chief hosted the FIFA president at the White House after the U.S. won the right to co-host the World Cup.

During the meeting, Infantino handed Trump red and yellow penalty cards and joked that the commander-in-chief could use them against the press.

The pair later met again in Davos in 2020, where they dined together.

Infantino was invited by Trump to the White House that same year for the signing of the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between several Middle Eastern countries and Israel.

Trump and Infantino appeared to grow closer during Trump's second term as the 2026 World Cup drew nearer.

Ahead of the world's biggest football tournament, Trump was handed the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize by Infantino in December 2025.

​In a press release detailing the award, FIFA credited Trump for his "pivotal role" in promoting peace between Israel and Palestine.

​The award was handed to Trump just months after Venezuelan activist María Corina Machado won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, despite the U.S. president insisting that he was deserving of the accolade.

Earlier this year, Infantino attended a meeting of Trump's Board of Peace and confirmed that FIFA would build an academy and a 20,000-seat stadium in Gaza.

"We don't have to just rebuild houses or schools or hospitals or roads," Infantino said at the event. "We also have to rebuild and build people, emotion, hope and trust. And this is what football, my sport, is about."

Once the world's biggest football tournament began, Infantino and Trump became embroiled in a slew of controversial moments.

During the contest Trump confirmed he had called Infantino personally after U.S. player Folarin Balogun was handed a red card during a match against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"I said, 'Gianni, I'd like to make a recommendation: Let the guy in the game,'" Trump said, recalling the phone call. "No, I didn't say that. I said I'd like to wage a complaint. And actually…I had no idea what was gonna happen."

Balogun was eventually allowed to play with the U.S. team in a match against Belgium, which ended in a victory for the latter country.

In a statement, Infantino said that the decision to allow Balogun to play was taken by the FIFA Disciplinary Committee and that all of FIFA's judicial bodies are "independent."​

Infantino also said that he explained to Trump that "there was an ongoing legal process involving FIFA's independent judicial bodies and that the case would be decided in due course by the competent bodies."​

When the tournament came to a close, Infantino was seen ushering Trump off stage when he awkwardly lingered on stage following Spain's victory over Argentina in the final.

A White House insider told The New York Post in July that Trump wanted Infantino to become the United Nations' next secretary general.

The insider claimed that Trump believes Infantino is "respected by everyone around the world" and that he has a "special ability to bring people together."

After the 2026 tournament eneded, Infantino came under fire over a plan to create a $20 billion subsidiary to run the World Cup and other events, with 20 percent of the subsidiary's shares being offered up to investors.

The plan was dropped after it drew anger and widespread international criticism.

In a scathing open letter, UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation called for an independent review into Infantino's plan, which they described as a "profound failure of judgement."

Some countries, including Mexico, Morocco and Argentina, have backed Infantino.

In a statement, FIFA claimed that there were attempts to "undermine" Infantino, who is seeking re-election in March next year.
